title: Insurance Marketplace Realities 2027: Construction
summary: WTW's 2027 forecast sees general liability flat to up 10%, auto and umbrella or excess up 5% to 15%, and workers' comp flat to up 5%. Workers' comp stays profitable while auto and excess face severity and nuclear verdicts. Data center megaprojects raise execution risk, and demand for subcontractor default insurance keeps outpacing market growth.
why: When excess gets expensive, trades buy less of it. Check umbrella limits against the project requirements at every renewal, not just at award.

title: A Better Tech Stack for the Trades
summary: Suffolk's venture arm maps technology for the trades by labor workflow, against a labor gap some put at 600,000 U.S. workers. It notes more than $500 million in recent workforce commitments from large companies and profiles tools for hiring, operations and payment. Suffolk marks its own portfolio companies.
why: Insurance compliance shows up on the map under getting paid. On a jobsite it belongs at the start, before a crew walks on.

title: Suffolk to embed AI engineers within construction projects
author: Matthew Thibault
summary: Suffolk's Jobsite of the Future program puts AI engineers in project meetings to work on design, schedule and process problems. Early tools spot drawing conflicts, track procurement and deliveries, and run an AI requisition process on a large Midwest project. Suffolk says its data lake holds about 293 terabytes of structured construction data.
why: Large GCs are wiring AI into project paperwork. Certificates and endorsements are paperwork too, and they need the same rigor about who checks the output.

title: US Construction Industry Update and Market Outlook: Mid-Year 2026
summary: Gallagher says infrastructure, data center, manufacturing and energy work keep construction busy despite labor shortages and rising claim severity. Its report cites AGC finding over 80% of contractors struggle to fill craft jobs. It puts typical excess liability increases at 5% to 30%, with builders risk renewals mostly flat outside catastrophe zones.
why: Short crews mean more new trades and more first-time certificates. That's when gaps slip in.

title: US and Canadian construction insurance are moving apart at the coverage level
author: Jhoanna Hines
summary: U.S. builders risk insurers have swapped the LEG3 defect clause for their own wordings with stricter defect definitions, higher deductibles and sublimits, while Canada keeps LEG3. Citing Marsh, the piece says well-managed U.S. projects saw 5% to 8% cuts late in 2025, even as U.S. casualty rates rose 9% in early 2026.
why: Same coverage name, different wording. Read the form, not the line on the certificate.

title: As Construction Booms, Insurers Draw Sharper Lines Between Good Risks and Bad
summary: Drawing on Aon's 2026 construction and surety report, the piece says terms favor well-managed risks and tighten for complex or catastrophe-exposed projects. Nuclear verdicts are shrinking excess capacity, with lead excess limits on large civil jobs down to about $5 million from $8 million to $10 million a year or two earlier.
why: Smaller excess layers mean more layers, and more policies to check for additional insured wording.

title: Seven Charged in $100 Million Workers' Comp Fraud in Florida
summary: Florida authorities charged seven people in an alleged $100 million workers' comp scheme. Prosecutors say shell companies bought thin coverage by underreporting payroll, then rented their certificates of insurance to subcontractors for a fee while crews were paid in cash. Ten insurers are named as alleged victims, and more than $2.4 million was seized.
why: A genuine certificate can sit on top of a policy that was never meant to cover the crew on your site. The COI alone can't tell you whose workers are insured.

title: Insurer prevails in coverage dispute over carpenter's death
author: Louise Esola
summary: An Illinois appellate court ruled that Mt. Hawley owes Stone Development no indemnity for a carpenter killed on his first day at a Waukegan hotel site, because the policy's employee injury exclusion applied. Stone had no workers' comp in force. The estate holds a $2.65 million agreed judgment; Mt. Hawley paid $250,000 toward it.
why: General liability usually excludes the contractor's own employees. If the certificate shows GL but workers' comp isn't active, that injury may have almost nowhere to land.

title: Idaho high court revives injured worker's lawsuit against contractor
author: Gavin Souter
summary: In Bauer v. Scott Myers and Sons Roofing, the Idaho Supreme Court revived a plumber's negligence suit against a roofer after a balcony railing the roofer allegedly reinstalled gave way. Whether one trade is shielded from suits by another trade's workers, the court said, turns on whether the GC controls the work, not on contract labels.
why: Trades on the same job can end up suing each other, which is exactly when real GL limits and correct additional insured endorsements get tested.

title: Florida Men Charged With Creating Sham Insurance Now Face Federal Indictment
author: William Rabb
summary: A federal grand jury indicted two Destin, Florida men tied to The Wave Insurance and Hydrogen Deep, neither licensed to write property and casualty coverage in Florida. Prosecutors allege they collected more than $651,000 in premiums and issued falsified certificates of insurance. Both pleaded not guilty; trial is set for December 14.
why: The carrier named on a certificate is worth checking against state insurance records. A COI can name a company that isn't allowed to write the coverage at all.

title: Zurich North American premiums rise 5% as construction business grows
author: Gavin Souter
summary: Zurich said its U.S. construction premiums grew 17% in the first nine months of 2026, helped by infrastructure and technology projects. North American property and casualty gross written premiums rose 5% to $18.69 billion while North American rates held flat. Global commercial rates fell 1%, mostly on softer large-property pricing.
why: Big carriers are growing construction books on flat rates. That's room for brokers to push for the endorsements project requirements ask for, not just price.
